## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Subha Sutta* (DN 10) is the tenth discourse in the *Dīghanikāya* of the Pali Canon. Set in Sāvatthī at Anāthapiṇḍika’s park, the sutta takes place shortly after the passing of the Buddha (*acira-parinibbute Bhagavati*) [Freedman 1977; Collins 1998; Allon 1997]. It represents the sole discourse in the first thirteen suttas of the *Dīghanikāya* where the Buddha's attendant Ānanda appears as the primary teacher, as well as the only passage in the collection depicting a member of the Saṅgha being formally invited to visit a layman's residence [Freedman 1977; Allon 1997]. The young brahmin Subha Todeyyaputta, residing temporarily in Sāvatthī, sends a young messenger to invite Ānanda to his dwelling in order to question him regarding the teachings praised and maintained by the Buddha [Allon 1997; Radich 2007].

In response to Subha's inquiry, Ānanda expounds the Dhamma structured under three aggregates or divisions (*khandha*): ethical conduct (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*) [Dhammapala et al. 1984; Freedman 1977; Radich 2007]. This tripartite schema provides the overarching framework for reciting the gradual path of training virtually verbatim from the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2) [Freedman 1977; Radich 2007; Hazra 1994]. As part of this sequence, the four *jhāna*s are delineated as the heart of noble concentration, leading Subha to remark that such noble concentration cannot be found among rival ascetics and brahmins [Polak 2011].

 Furthermore, DharmaNexus aligns passages of the discourse cross-linguistically with Sanskrit and Tibetan Vinaya literature—notably the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Vinayavastu*—as well as the *Daśabalasūtra* and *Śrāvakabhūmi* [DharmaNexus].
